claims.source: Consistent with previous reports of Pim1 and Pim2 being the major PIM kinases in T cells (Mikkers et al., 2004; Fox et al., 2005), Pim3 mRNA was only expressed at very low levels in naive and activated CD8 T cells (Figure 1C), with PIM3 protein not detected at all by mass spectrometry (Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics data showing absence of PIM3 protein.

claims.claim: PIM1 and PIM2 have similar substrate selectivity and functional redundancy.
claims.source: PIM1 and PIM2 have similar substrate selectivity and hence functional redundancy (Mikkers et al., 2004; Bullock et al., 2005; Fox et al., 2005; Peng et al., 2007; Warfel and Kraft, 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by multiple literature citations establishing this property of PIM kinases.

claims.claim: There were normal proportions of peripheral T cells in spleens of Pim dKO mice.
claims.source: There were normal proportions of peripheral T cells in spleens of Pim dKO mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) similar to what has been reported previously in Pim dKO mice on an FVB/N genetic background (Mikkers et al., 2004), although the total number of T cells and splenocytes was lower than in age/sex matched wild-type (WT) mouse spleens (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data showing T cell proportions in spleens, and is consistent with previous literature.

claims.claim: The total number of T cells in Pim dKO mouse spleens was lower than in age/sex matched wild-type mouse spleens.
claims.source: There were normal proportions of peripheral T cells in spleens of Pim dKO mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) similar to what has been reported previously in Pim dKO mice on an FVB/N genetic background (Mikkers et al., 2004), although the total number of T cells and splenocytes was lower than in age/sex matched wild-type (WT) mouse spleens (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data showing reduced total T cell numbers in Pim dKO spleens.

claims.claim: The total number of splenocytes in Pim dKO mice was lower than in age/sex matched wild-type mice.
claims.source: There were normal proportions of peripheral T cells in spleens of Pim dKO mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) similar to what has been reported previously in Pim dKO mice on an FVB/N genetic background (Mikkers et al., 2004), although the total number of T cells and splenocytes was lower than in age/sex matched wild-type (WT) mouse spleens (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data showing reduced total splenocyte numbers.

claims.claim: The reduced total number of T cells and splenocytes in Pim dKO mice was likely the result of these mice being smaller in size.
claims.source: This was not attributable to any one cell type (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; James et al., 2021) but was instead likely the result of these mice being smaller in size, a phenotype that has previously been reported in Pim1/2/3 triple KO mice (Mikkers et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the data and comparison with previous literature showing smaller size in PIM-deficient mice.

claims.claim: Pim dKO CD4 and CD8 T cells showed a normal increase in cell size in response to in vitro immune activation with αCD3/αCD28 agonist antibodies.
claims.source: We tested how Pim dKO T cells respond to immune activation and observed a normal increase in cell size in response to in vitro immune activation with αCD3/αCD28 agonist antibodies (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data showing FSC-A SSC-A profiles in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: 24 hr αCD3/αCD28 activated Pim dKO CD4 and CD8 T cells normally upregulated expression of CD25, CD44 and CD71.
claims.source: 24 hr αCD3/αCD28 activated Pim dKO CD4 and CD8 T cells also normally upregulated expression of established markers of T cell activation including CD25, CD44 and the transferrin receptor CD71 (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data showing activation marker expression in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: 24 hr TCR-activated Pim dKO CD8 T cells produced normal levels of IFNγ.
claims.source: 24 hr TCR-activated Pim dKO CD8 T cells also produced normal levels of the key effector cytokine IFNγ (Figure 1E) and there was no discernible difference in TCR-driven proliferation between WT and Pim dKO T cells over 3 days in culture (Figure 1F and J).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data showing IFNγ production in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: There was no discernible difference in TCR-driven proliferation between WT and Pim dKO T cells over 3 days in culture.
claims.source: 24 hr TCR-activated Pim dKO CD8 T cells also produced normal levels of the key effector cytokine IFNγ (Figure 1E) and there was no discernible difference in TCR-driven proliferation between WT and Pim dKO T cells over 3 days in culture (Figure 1F and J).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by CTV proliferation assay data shown in Figures 1F and 1J.

claims.claim: High-resolution mass spectrometry quantified expression of >7000 proteins in 24 hr αCD3/αCD28 activated WT and Pim dKO CD4 and CD8 T cells.
claims.source: These experiments quantified expression of >7000 proteins but found no substantial quantitative or qualitative differences in protein content or proteome composition in activated WT versus Pim dKO CD4 and CD8 T cells (Figure 1G–H) (Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics data showing the number of proteins quantified.

claims.claim: There were no substantial quantitative or qualitative differences in protein content or proteome composition in 24 hr activated WT versus Pim dKO CD4 and CD8 T cells.
claims.source: These experiments quantified expression of >7000 proteins but found no substantial quantitative or qualitative differences in protein content or proteome composition in activated WT versus Pim dKO CD4 and CD8 T cells (Figure 1G–H) (Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics data showing minimal differences between genotypes, as shown in Figures 1G-H.

claims.claim: PIM kinases do not play an important unique role in the signalling pathways used by the TCR and CD28 to control T cell activation.
claims.source: Collectively, these results indicate that PIM kinases do not play an important unique role in the signalling pathways used by the TCR and CD28 to control T cell activation.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the data showing no substantial differences in activation markers, proliferation, or proteome composition between WT and Pim dKO T cells.

claims.claim: A previous study reported that Pim dKO naive T cells cultured in IL-7 died in response to rapamycin treatment.
claims.source: This previous study showed Pim dKO, but not WT, naive T cells cultured in IL-7 died in response to rapamycin treatment.
claims.evidence: The claim references findings from a previous study (Fox et al., 2005).

claims.claim: A previous study showed that rapamycin synergised with Pim1/Pim2-deficiency to substantially reduce TCR-driven activation and proliferation.
claims.source: It was also shown that rapamycin synergised with Pim1/Pim2-deficiency to substantially reduce TCR-driven activation and proliferation (Fox et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: The claim references findings from a previous study.

claims.claim: There was no impact of Pim1/Pim2-deficiency on the ability of naive CD8 T cells cultured with IL-7 to survive in response to rapamycin treatment.
claims.source: However, we found no impact of Pim1/Pim2-deficiency on the ability of naive CD8 T cells cultured with IL-7 to survive in response to rapamycin treatment (Figure 1I).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cell viability data shown in Figure 1I.

claims.claim: There was no difference in the effect of rapamycin on mean division number in αCD3/αCD28 activated Pim dKO versus WT CD8 T cells.
claims.source: Furthermore, we found no difference in the effect of rapamycin on mean division number in αCD3/αCD28 activated Pim dKO versus WT CD8 T cells (Figure 1J).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by proliferation data shown in Figure 1J.

claims.claim: PIM 1 and PIM2 are rapidly and strongly expressed in response to immune activation.
claims.source: Collectively, these data show that PIM 1 and PIM2 are rapidly and strongly expressed in response to immune activation, but they are dispensable for the antigen receptor and CD28-driven proteome remodelling that initiates T cell clonal expansion and differentiation.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics and RNAseq data showing rapid induction of PIM kinases after activation.

claims.claim: PIM1 and PIM2 are dispensable for the antigen receptor and CD28-driven proteome remodelling that initiates T cell clonal expansion and differentiation.
claims.source: Collectively, these data show that PIM 1 and PIM2 are rapidly and strongly expressed in response to immune activation, but they are dispensable for the antigen receptor and CD28-driven proteome remodelling that initiates T cell clonal expansion and differentiation.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the data showing no substantial differences in proteome composition or activation phenotypes between WT and Pim dKO T cells.

claims.claim: There is no evidence that mTORc1 was substituting for Pim1 and Pim2 loss in TCR-activated T cells.
claims.source: We also found no evidence that mTORc1 was substituting for Pim1 and Pim2 loss.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the rapamycin experiments showing no differential effect in Pim dKO versus WT cells.

claims.claim: IL-2 and IL-15 upregulate PIM1 and PIM2 expression in antigen primed CD8 T cells.
claims.source: In this context, PIM1 and PIM2 kinase expression is regulated by the cytokines IL-2 and IL-15 which are key to shaping CD8 T cell effector and memory cell differentiation, respectively (Weninger et al., 2001; Cornish et al., 2006; Buck et al., 2016). Both IL-2 and IL-15 upregulate PIM1 and PIM2 expression in antigen primed CD8 T cells (Figure 2A) and are required to sustain PIM1 and PIM2 expression (Rollings et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2A and is consistent with previous literature.

claims.claim: IL-2 and IL-15 are required to sustain PIM1 and PIM2 expression in antigen primed CD8 T cells.
claims.source: Both IL-2 and IL-15 upregulate PIM1 and PIM2 expression in antigen primed CD8 T cells (Figure 2A) and are required to sustain PIM1 and PIM2 expression (Rollings et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data and a literature citation.

claims.claim: PIM1 and PIM2 mediate IL-15 induced proliferation of gut intra-epithelial lymphocytes (IEL).
claims.source: Previous work has shown that PIM1 and PIM2 mediate IL-15 induced proliferation of gut intra-epithelial lymphocytes (IEL; James et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: The claim references findings from a previous study.

claims.claim: Antigen experienced WT CD8 T cells show an ~90-fold expansion between days 2 and 6 of culture in IL-15.
claims.source: Antigen experienced WT CD8 T cells show a robust proliferative response to IL-15 such that there is an ~90-fold expansion of the CD8 T cells between days 2 and 6 of culture (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cell counting data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Immune activated Pim dKO CD8 T cells showed a moderate proliferative disadvantage in IL-15, resulting in an ~4-fold difference in total cell number by day 6 of culture.
claims.source: Immune activated Pim dKO CD8 T cells also proliferated strongly in response to IL-15, but showed a moderate proliferative disadvantage resulting in an ~4-fold difference in total cell number by day 6 of the culture (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cell counting data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: There was no impact of Pim1/Pim2-deficiency on the ability of IL-15 to sustain CD8 T cell viability.
claims.source: There was no impact of Pim1/Pim2-deficiency on the ability of IL-15 to sustain CD8 T cell viability (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by viability data shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: RNAseq analysis quantified ~14,000 unique polyA+ RNA in IL-15 expanded WT and Pim dKO CD8 T cells.
claims.source: The RNAseq analysis quantified ~14,000 unique polyA+ RNA and using a cut off of >1.5 fold-change and q-value <0.05 we saw that the abundance of 381 polyA+ RNA was modified by Pim1/Pim2-deficiency (Figure 2E) (Supplementary file 2A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq data showing the number of RNA quantified.

claims.claim: The abundance of 381 polyA+ RNA was modified by Pim1/Pim2-deficiency in IL-15 expanded CD8 T cells (FC >1.5, q<0.05).
claims.source: The RNAseq analysis quantified ~14,000 unique polyA+ RNA and using a cut off of >1.5 fold-change and q-value <0.05 we saw that the abundance of 381 polyA+ RNA was modified by Pim1/Pim2-deficiency (Figure 2E) (Supplementary file 2A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq data showing differentially expressed RNA.

claims.claim: Only 72 substantially expressed protein coding mRNA were differentially expressed in Pim dKO versus WT IL-15 expanded CD8 T cells.
claims.source: Of the 381 RNA that were detected as differentially expressed (FC >1.5, q<0.05) only ~30% were detected with an average expression over 10 transcripts per million (TPM), of these gene ~36% were non-coding RNA, uncharacterised genes or pseudogenes, leaving only 72 substantially expressed protein coding mRNA that were differentially expressed in Pim dKO versus WT IL-15 expanded CD8 T cells (Supplementary file 2B).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on analysis of RNAseq data filtering for expression level and gene type.

claims.claim: Pim1/Pim2-deficiency has very little effect on IL-15 induced protein-coding mRNA expression in differentiated T cells.
claims.source: These data indicate that Pim1/Pim2-deficiency has very little effect on IL-15 induced protein-coding mRNA expression in differentiated T cells.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the RNAseq data showing only 72 substantially expressed protein-coding mRNA were differentially expressed.

claims.claim: Pim1/Pim2-deficiency did not decrease expression of mRNA levels for CD62L (Sell), Ccr7 and S1pr1 in IL-15 expanded CD8 T cells.
claims.source: We found that Pim1/Pim2-deficiency did not decrease expression of mRNA levels for critical memory T cell genes such as the adhesion molecules and chemokine receptors, Sell (CD62L), Ccr7 and S1pr1 that direct the trafficking of CD8 T cells to secondary lymphoid tissue. (Figure 2F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: Pim1/Pim2-deficiency did not reduce expression of mRNA for the key memory cell transcription factors Tcf7, Foxo1, Foxo3, Klf2, and Id3 in IL-15 expanded CD8 T cells.
claims.source: Pim1/Pim2-deficiency also did not reduce expression of mRNA for the key memory cell transcription factors Tcf7, Foxo1, Foxo3 Klf2, and Id3. (Figure 2G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 2G.

claims.claim: There were small increases in expression of Klf2, Id3, and Ccr7 mRNA in Pim dKO versus WT IL-15 expanded CD8 T cells.
claims.source: Indeed, if anything, there were small increases in expression of the Klf2, Id3, and Ccr7 mRNA in Pim dKO versus WT IL-15 expanded CD8 T cells (Figure 2F and G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figures 2F and 2G.

claims.claim: Proteomics analysis quantified expression of ~6900 total proteins in IL-15 expanded WT and Pim dKO CD8 T cells.
claims.source: Critically, when the proteomes of IL-15 expanded WT and Pim dKO CD8 T cells were analysed and expression of ~6900 total proteins quantified, there were no major changes in the proteomes between WT and Pim dKO IL-15 expanded CD8 T cells (Figure 2H, Supplementary file 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics data showing the number of proteins quantified.

claims.claim: There were no major changes in the proteomes between WT and Pim dKO IL-15 expanded CD8 T cells.
claims.source: Critically, when the proteomes of IL-15 expanded WT and Pim dKO CD8 T cells were analysed and expression of ~6900 total proteins quantified, there were no major changes in the proteomes between WT and Pim dKO IL-15 expanded CD8 T cells (Figure 2H, Supplementary file 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 2H.

claims.claim: The mitochondrial proteome composition of IL-15 expanded WT and Pim dKO CD8 T cells were indistinguishable.
claims.source: Of note, the mitochondrial proteome composition of IL-15 expanded WT and Pim dKO CD8 T cells were indistinguishable (Figure 2I and J).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics data showing mitochondrial protein expression in Figures 2I and 2J.

claims.claim: IL-15 controls memory T cells via mitochondrial remodelling to support energy production via oxidative phosphorylation and fatty acid oxidation.
claims.source: This is pertinent because one key feature of how IL-15 controls memory T cells is via mitochondrial remodelling to support energy production via oxidative phosphorylation and fatty acid oxidation (Buck et al., 2016), and it has been described that PIM kinases can control mitochondrial phenotypes in cancer cell lines and cardiomyocytes (Din et al., 2013; Chauhan et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by literature citations describing IL-15's role in mitochondrial remodelling.

claims.claim: PIM kinases can control mitochondrial phenotypes in cancer cell lines and cardiomyocytes.
claims.source: This is pertinent because one key feature of how IL-15 controls memory T cells is via mitochondrial remodelling to support energy production via oxidative phosphorylation and fatty acid oxidation (Buck et al., 2016), and it has been described that PIM kinases can control mitochondrial phenotypes in cancer cell lines and cardiomyocytes (Din et al., 2013; Chauhan et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by literature citations.

claims.claim: PIM1 and PIM2 do not drive IL-15-mediated metabolic or differentiation programs in antigen-primed CD8 T cells.
claims.source: These data show that PIM1 and PIM2 do not drive IL-15-mediated metabolic or differentiation programs in antigen-primed CD8 T cells.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the proteomics and RNAseq data showing minimal differences between WT and Pim dKO IL-15 expanded cells.

claims.claim: The copy numbers per cell of PIM1 protein is considerably higher in actively expanding antigen-activated CD8 cells maintained with IL-2 compared to IL-15.
claims.source: IL-2 promotes the expression of PIM1 and PIM2 kinases (Figure 2A), and in this context, we noted that the copy numbers per cell of PIM1 protein is considerably higher in actively expanding antigen-activated CD8 cells maintained with IL-2 compared to IL-15 (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Pim dKO antigen activated CD8 T cells responded normally to IL-2 to induce STAT5 Y694 phosphorylation.
claims.source: The data show that Pim dKO antigen activated CD8 T cells responded normally to IL-2 to induce STAT5 Y694 phosphorylation (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Pim dKO CD8 T cells express normal levels of CD25 (IL-2-receptor alpha chain).
claims.source: They also express normal levels of the IL-2-receptor alpha chain, CD25, (Figure 3C), which is sustained by STAT5.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Antigen activated WT CD8 T cells have an ~270-fold expansion between days 2 and 6 of culture in saturating IL-2 concentrations.
claims.source: Antigen activated WT CD8 T cells have a strong survival and proliferative response to IL-2 producing an ~270-fold expansion between days 2 and 6 of culture in saturating IL-2 concentrations (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cell counting data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: There was no impact of Pim1/Pim2-deficiency on the ability of IL-2 to maintain CD8 T cell viability.
claims.source: There was no impact of Pim1/Pim2-deficiency on the ability of IL-2 to maintain CD8 T cell viability (Figure 3E) and Pim dKO cells CD8 T cells cultured in IL-2 proliferated robustly.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by viability data shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: Pim dKO CD8 T cells cultured in IL-2 exhibited a very mild proliferative disadvantage resulting in an ~2-fold difference in total cell number by day 6 of culture.
claims.source: They did however exhibit a very mild proliferative disadvantage resulting in an ~2-fold difference in total cell number by day 6 of the culture (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cell counting data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Expression of activation markers CD44 and CD71 in IL-2-expanded CTL were similar between WT and Pim dKO CD8 T cells on days 3 and 6 of co-cultures.
claims.source: Expression of activation markers CD44 and CD71 in IL-2-expanded CTL were similar between WT and Pim dKO CD8 T cells on days 3 and 6 of co-cultures (Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: WT CTL downregulated expression of CD62L in IL-2, whereas Pim dKO CTL sustained higher CD62L expression.
claims.source: However, one consistent difference between IL-2 maintained WT and Pim dKO CD8 T cells is that WT CTL downregulated expression of CD62L (L-selectin, Sell), whereas the Pim dKO CTL sustained higher CD62L expression (Figure 3G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3G.

claims.claim: IL-2 maintained Pim dKO CTL were smaller and less granular than the corresponding WT CTL.
claims.source: We also noted that IL-2 maintained Pim dKO CTL had reduced forward and side scatter properties, revealing that they were smaller and less granular than the corresponding WT CTL (Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data showing FSC-A and SSC-A in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: Proteomics analysis quantified expression of ~6900 proteins in day 6 IL-2 cultured WT and Pim dKO CTL.
claims.source: These analyses quantified expression of ~6900 proteins and showed a small decrease in the total protein mass of IL-2 maintained Pim dKO CD8 T cells compared to WT cells (Figure 4A, Supplementary file 4).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics data showing the number of proteins quantified.

claims.claim: There was a small decrease in the total protein mass of IL-2 maintained Pim dKO CD8 T cells compared to WT cells.
claims.source: These analyses quantified expression of ~6900 proteins and showed a small decrease in the total protein mass of IL-2 maintained Pim dKO CD8 T cells compared to WT cells (Figure 4A, Supplementary file 4).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: 513 proteins were down-regulated (>1.5 fold-change, q<0.05) in Pim dKO CTL compared to WT CTL.
claims.source: The data showed down-regulation of the expression of 513 proteins (>1.5 fold-change, q<0.05) in Pim dKO CTL along with increased copy numbers of 33 proteins (Figure 4B, Supplementary file 4).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: 33 proteins had increased copy numbers (>1.5 fold-change, q<0.05) in Pim dKO CTL compared to WT CTL.
claims.source: The data showed down-regulation of the expression of 513 proteins (>1.5 fold-change, q<0.05) in Pim dKO CTL along with increased copy numbers of 33 proteins (Figure 4B, Supplementary file 4).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: The transcription factor profile of Pim dKO T cells was consistent with that of an effector CTL with high levels of TBX21 and low levels of TCF1.
claims.source: The transcription factor profile of Pim dKO T cells was consistent with that of an effector CTL with high levels of TBX21 and low levels of TCF1 (Tcf7; Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: Pim dKO T cells exhibited an effector-like mitochondrial proteome profile.
claims.source: Pim dKO T cells also exhibited an effector-like mitochondrial proteome profile (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Pim dKO CTL had lower levels of the glucose transporters SLC2A1 and SLC2A3 compared to WT CTL.
claims.source: These included lower levels of the glucose transporters, SLC2A1 and SLC2A3 (GLUT1 and GLUT3; Figure 4D) which are the major glucose transporters in CD8 T cells (Hukelmann et al., 2016) and are key for enabling T cells to fuel high rates of glycolysis and protein O-GlcNAcylation required to support effector functions (Chang et al., 2015; Swamy et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 4D and is consistent with previous literature on glucose transporter function.

claims.claim: SLC2A1 and SLC2A3 are the major glucose transporters in CD8 T cells.
claims.source: These included lower levels of the glucose transporters, SLC2A1 and SLC2A3 (GLUT1 and GLUT3; Figure 4D) which are the major glucose transporters in CD8 T cells (Hukelmann et al., 2016) and are key for enabling T cells to fuel high rates of glycolysis and protein O-GlcNAcylation required to support effector functions (Chang et al., 2015; Swamy et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by literature citations.

claims.claim: Glucose transporters are key for enabling T cells to fuel high rates of glycolysis and protein O-GlcNAcylation required to support effector functions.
claims.source: These included lower levels of the glucose transporters, SLC2A1 and SLC2A3 (GLUT1 and GLUT3; Figure 4D) which are the major glucose transporters in CD8 T cells (Hukelmann et al., 2016) and are key for enabling T cells to fuel high rates of glycolysis and protein O-GlcNAcylation required to support effector functions (Chang et al., 2015; Swamy et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by literature citations.

claims.claim: Pim dKO CTL had decreased expression of proteins involved in fatty acid and cholesterol biosynthesis including SCD2, HMGCS1, MVK, IDI1, FDPS, FDFT1, and SQLE.
claims.source: Pim dKO CTL also had decreased expression of a number of proteins involved in fatty acid and cholesterol biosynthesis including SCD2, HMGCS1, MVK, IDI1, FDPS, FDFT1, and SQLE (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: Pim dKO CD8 cells had reduced levels of multiple granzymes, perforin, IFNγ, and TNFα.
claims.source: Another striking observation was that the Pim dKO CD8 cells had reduced levels of a number of key effector proteins including multiple granzymes, perforin, IFNγ, and TNFα (Figure 4F–H).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics data shown in Figures 4F-H.

claims.claim: Flow cytometric analysis confirmed reduced levels of Granzyme B and IFNγ in IL-2 expanded Pim dKO CTL.
claims.source: Orthogonal flow cytometric analysis of Granzyme B and IFNγ levels confirmed reduced levels of these effector molecule in IL-2 expanded Pim dKO CTL, although IFNγ protein is only lowly produced in IL-2 maintained CTL (Figure 4I).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4I.

claims.claim: 24 hr treatment with pan-PIM kinases inhibitors PIM447 or AZD1208 caused reductions in cell proliferation, cell size, cell granularity, fatty acid biosynthesis proteins SCD1-3, glucose transporters SLC2A1 and SLC2A3, and Granzyme B expression in IL-2 maintained WT CTL.
claims.source: When IL-2 maintained WT CTL were treated for 24 hr with the pan-PIM kinases inhibitors PIM447 or AZD1208 we saw reductions in cell proliferation, cell size, cell granularity, fatty acid biosynthesis proteins SCD1-3, glucose transporters SLC2A1, SLC2A3 and a reduction in Granzyme B expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–E, Supplementary file 5).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics and flow cytometry data from PIM kinase inhibitor experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The pattern of proteome remodelling in Pim dKO CTL had some phenotypic features in common with previously reported changes following inhibition of mTORc1 in CTL.
claims.source: The pattern of proteome remodelling in Pim dKO CTL had some phenotypic features in common with the previously reported changes that occur following inhibition of the Serine/Threonine kinase mTORc1 in CTL (Hukelmann et al., 2016; Howden et al., 2019). These included: increased expression of PDCD4 and decreased expression of cholesterol biosynthesis enzymes and effector molecules including granzymes, perforin, IFNγ and TNFα (Hukelmann et al., 2016; Howden et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on comparison of the current proteomics data with previous literature on mTORc1 inhibition effects.

claims.claim: mTORc1 activity in CTL is acutely sensitive to reduced availability of glucose.
claims.source: In this respect, mTORc1 activity in CTL is acutely sensitive to reduced availability of glucose (Rolf et al., 2013) and the reduced expression of glucose transporters in Pim dKO T cells might predict that these cells would have lower activity of mTORc1.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a literature citation.

claims.claim: Pim1/Pim2-deficiency modestly reduced mTORc1 activity in IL-2 maintained CD8 T cells.
claims.source: These data show a modest reduction of mTORc1 activity in the Pim dKO T cells (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data showing reduced pS6K T389 in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: Pim1/Pim2-deficiency reduced IL-2 induced mTORc1-dependent phosphorylation of S6 in CD8 T cells.
claims.source: These data also show that Pim1/Pim2-deficiency reduced IL-2 induced mTORc1-dependent phosphorylation of S6 but did not compromise the ability of the Pim dKO cells to phosphorylate S6 in response to phorbol esters and calcium ionophores; pharmacological activators that induce RSK mediated S6 phosphorylation (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data showing reduced pS6 in Pim dKO cells in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: Pim1/Pim2-deficiency did not compromise the ability of CD8 T cells to phosphorylate S6 in response to phorbol esters and calcium ionophores.
claims.source: These data also show that Pim1/Pim2-deficiency reduced IL-2 induced mTORc1-dependent phosphorylation of S6 but did not compromise the ability of the Pim dKO cells to phosphorylate S6 in response to phorbol esters and calcium ionophores; pharmacological activators that induce RSK mediated S6 phosphorylation (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data showing normal pS6 response to PdBU/ionomycin in Pim dKO cells in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: Decreased glucose availability or inhibition of mTORc1 prevents the downregulation of CD62L that normally accompanies IL-2-induced CTL differentiation.
claims.source: Previously, it has been shown that decreased glucose availability or inhibition of mTORc1 prevents the downregulation of CD62L that normally accompanies IL-2-induced CTL differentiation (Sinclair et al., 2008; Finlay et al., 2012).

results.result: PIM1 and PIM2 kinases are rapidly induced following TCR engagement in CD8 T cells. PIM1 protein is strongly induced within 3 hours and sustained at 24 hours, while PIM2 appears at 9 hours and is also sustained. This induction occurs at both protein and mRNA levels, with Pim1 and Pim2 mRNA being very lowly expressed in naive cells and strongly upregulated by immune activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C8 are well-supported by quantitative proteomics and RNAseq data from multiple experimental systems (OT1 cells with cognate peptide and polyclonal activation with αCD3/αCD28). The temporal dynamics are clearly documented in Figure 1A-C, and the data are consistent with published datasets (Marchingo et al., 2020; Spinelli et al., 2021).

results.result: Pim1 and Pim2 are the major PIM kinases in T cells, with Pim3 showing minimal expression. Pim3 mRNA is expressed at very low levels in naive and activated CD8 T cells, and PIM3 protein is not detected by mass spectrometry.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C11 are supported by both RNAseq and proteomics data showing low/absent Pim3 expression (Figure 1C, Supplementary file 1). This is consistent with previous literature (Mikkers et al., 2004; Fox et al., 2005), providing converging evidence for the conclusion.

results.result: Pim dKO mice have normal proportions of peripheral T cells in spleens, but reduced total numbers of T cells and splenocytes compared to wild-type mice. This reduction is attributed to the smaller body size of Pim dKO mice rather than specific immune defects.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C16 are supported by flow cytometry data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-C) and are consistent with previous reports in Pim dKO mice on different genetic backgrounds. The inference about body size (C16) is reasonable given the data distribution across cell types and literature precedent, though direct body weight measurements are not shown.

results.result: PIM kinases are dispensable for TCR and CD28-driven T cell activation. Pim dKO T cells show normal increases in cell size, upregulation of activation markers (CD25, CD44, CD71), IFNγ production, and proliferation over 3 days. High-resolution proteomics of >7000 proteins revealed no substantial differences in protein content or proteome composition between activated WT and Pim dKO T cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C23 are strongly supported by multiple orthogonal approaches: flow cytometry for phenotypic markers (Figure 1D-E), CTV proliferation assays (Figure 1F, J), and comprehensive proteomics analysis (Figure 1G-H, Supplementary file 1). The conclusion (C23) is a reasonable inference from the collective data showing no substantial functional or molecular differences.

results.result: The current study contradicts previous reports about PIM kinase and mTORc1 interactions in T cell activation. Unlike Fox et al. (2005), the authors find no impact of Pim1/Pim2-deficiency on naive T cell survival in IL-7 plus rapamycin, and no differential effect of rapamycin on TCR-driven proliferation in Pim dKO versus WT cells, providing no evidence that mTORc1 substitutes for PIM kinase loss.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C27 and C30 are supported by experimental data (Figure 1I-J) that directly test the hypotheses from prior work. The discrepancy with Fox et al. (2005) is clearly documented. However, the reasons for the discrepancy are not explored (different genetic backgrounds, culture conditions, etc.), which limits mechanistic understanding.

results.result: IL-2 and IL-15 upregulate and sustain PIM1 and PIM2 expression in antigen-primed CD8 T cells. Previous work has shown that PIM kinases mediate IL-15-induced proliferation of gut intraepithelial lymphocytes.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C32 are supported by western blot data (Figure 2A) and literature citations. C33 is a citation of prior work (James et al., 2021) and is appropriately attributed. The data provide context for investigating PIM kinase function in cytokine-driven T cell differentiation.

results.result: In IL-15, WT CD8 T cells show robust proliferation (~90-fold expansion between days 2-6), while Pim dKO cells show a moderate proliferative disadvantage (~4-fold difference by day 6). However, Pim1/Pim2-deficiency does not affect IL-15's ability to sustain CD8 T cell viability.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C36 are supported by cell counting and viability data (Figure 2C-D). The proliferative disadvantage is modest but reproducible. The lack of viability defect suggests the proliferation difference is not due to increased cell death.

results.result: Pim1/Pim2-deficiency has minimal impact on IL-15-driven transcriptional programs in CD8 T cells. RNAseq quantified ~14,000 RNA, with 381 differentially expressed (FC >1.5, q<0.05), but only 72 were substantially expressed protein-coding mRNA. Expression of key memory cell genes (Sell, Ccr7, S1pr1, Tcf7, Foxo1, Foxo3, Klf2, Id3) was not decreased, with small increases in Klf2, Id3, and Ccr7.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C43 are supported by comprehensive RNAseq analysis (Figure 2E-G, Supplementary file 2). The filtering approach to identify substantially expressed protein-coding genes is appropriate. The data convincingly show that PIM kinases do not control IL-15-driven transcriptional programs for memory differentiation.

results.result: PIM kinases do not drive IL-15-mediated metabolic or differentiation programs in antigen-primed CD8 T cells. Proteomics analysis of ~6900 proteins showed no major changes between WT and Pim dKO IL-15 expanded cells, including indistinguishable mitochondrial proteome composition, despite IL-15's known role in mitochondrial remodeling and prior reports of PIM kinase effects on mitochondria in other cell types.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C49 are strongly supported by comprehensive proteomics data (Figure 2H-J, Supplementary file 3). The mitochondrial analysis is particularly important given the known role of IL-15 in mitochondrial remodeling (C47) and prior reports of PIM effects on mitochondria (C48). The conclusion (C49) is well-justified by the data.

results.result: PIM1 protein levels are considerably higher in IL-2 versus IL-15 expanded CD8 T cells. Pim dKO cells respond normally to IL-2 for STAT5 phosphorylation and CD25 expression. In IL-2, WT cells show ~270-fold expansion (days 2-6), while Pim dKO cells show a very mild proliferative disadvantage (~2-fold difference) without viability defects. Activation markers CD44 and CD71 are similar between genotypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C56 are supported by proteomics (Figure 3A), flow cytometry (Figure 3B-C, F), and cell counting data (Figure 3D-E). The differential PIM1 expression in IL-2 vs IL-15 (C50) provides important context for the subsequent functional analyses. The mild proliferative defect in IL-2 contrasts with the more pronounced effect in IL-15.

results.result: IL-2 maintained Pim dKO CTL show distinct phenotypic differences from WT: they sustain higher CD62L expression (while WT downregulate it) and are smaller and less granular based on flow cytometry scatter properties.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C58 are supported by flow cytometry data (Figure 3F-G). The sustained CD62L expression in Pim dKO cells is a consistent and striking phenotype that suggests altered trafficking properties. The reduced size/granularity (C58) is consistent with subsequent proteomics findings of reduced protein content.

results.result: Proteomics analysis of day 6 IL-2 cultured CTL quantified ~6900 proteins and revealed a small decrease in total protein mass in Pim dKO cells. 513 proteins were downregulated and 33 upregulated (FC >1.5, q<0.05). Despite these changes, Pim dKO cells maintain an effector CTL transcription factor profile (high TBX21, low TCF1) and effector-like mitochondrial proteome.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C64 are supported by comprehensive proteomics data (Figure 4A-C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 4). The data show that while Pim dKO cells have quantitative proteome differences, they retain core effector characteristics. This is important for interpreting the functional significance of PIM kinase loss.

results.result: Pim dKO CTL have reduced expression of key metabolic and effector proteins including glucose transporters (SLC2A1, SLC2A3), fatty acid/cholesterol biosynthesis enzymes (SCD2, HMGCS1, MVK, IDI1, FDPS, FDFT1, SQLE), and cytolytic effector molecules (granzymes, perforin, IFNγ, TNFα). These findings are confirmed by flow cytometry and recapitulated by acute treatment with pan-PIM kinase inhibitors.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C71 are strongly supported by proteomics data (Figure 4D-H, Supplementary file 4), orthogonal flow cytometry validation (Figure 4I), and pharmacological inhibitor experiments (Figure 4—figure supplement 2). The convergence of genetic and pharmacological approaches strengthens the conclusions. The biological significance is enhanced by citations establishing the importance of these proteins for T cell function (C66-C67).

results.result: The proteome changes in Pim dKO CTL share features with mTORc1 inhibition, including increased PDCD4 and decreased cholesterol biosynthesis enzymes and effector molecules. mTORc1 activity in CTL is known to be sensitive to glucose availability, suggesting a potential mechanistic link through reduced glucose transporter expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C73 are supported by comparison with published data on mTORc1 inhibition (Hukelmann et al., 2016; Howden et al., 2019) and literature on mTORc1 glucose sensitivity (Rolf et al., 2013). This provides important mechanistic context, though the causal relationship is not directly tested here.

results.result: Pim1/Pim2-deficiency modestly reduces mTORc1 activity in IL-2 maintained CD8 T cells, as shown by reduced phosphorylation of S6K T389 and S6 S235/236. However, Pim dKO cells retain the ability to phosphorylate S6 in response to phorbol esters and calcium ionophores (RSK-mediated pathway).
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C76 are supported by western blot (Figure 6A) and flow cytometry data (Figure 6B). The specificity for mTORc1-dependent phosphorylation (C75) versus RSK-mediated phosphorylation (C76) is demonstrated by appropriate controls. The modest reduction in mTORc1 activity provides a mechanistic link to the proteome changes.

results.result: CD62L (Sell) mRNA expression is increased in IL-2 maintained Pim dKO CTL, along with increased expression of the transcription factor Klf2 and its targets Ccr7 and S1pr1. This is consistent with prior work showing that glucose limitation or mTORc1 inhibition prevents CD62L downregulation during IL-2-induced CTL differentiation.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C81 are supported by RNAseq data (Figures 5B, 6C-D) and literature citations (Sinclair et al., 2008; Finlay et al., 2012). The transcriptional mechanism through KLF2 (C79) is based on established knowledge and is consistent with the coordinate upregulation of KLF2 target genes. This provides a mechanistic explanation for the sustained CD62L protein expression observed in C57.

results.result: PIM kinases are required for normal reprogramming of CTL trafficking. CD62L, CCR7, and S1PR1 control T cell homing to secondary lymphoid tissue, and their loss during activation redirects effector cells to peripheral tissues. Pim dKO CTL, but not WT CTL, retain substantial capacity to home to secondary lymphoid organs (lymph nodes and spleen) after adoptive transfer.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C86 are supported by adoptive transfer experiments (Figure 6E) and established knowledge of homing receptor function (C82-C84, supported by literature). The in vivo functional consequence (C85) directly demonstrates that the molecular changes in homing receptor expression translate to altered trafficking behavior. This is a key functional validation of the molecular findings.

results.result: PIM kinases show selective roles in CD8 T cell differentiation: they have no effect on antigen receptor/co-stimulation programs, very little impact on IL-15-driven programs in memory cells, but are required for IL-2 programming of effector CD8 T cell differentiation.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C89 represent the major conclusions synthesized from the comprehensive dataset. They are well-supported by the collective evidence from proteomics, RNAseq, and functional assays across different stimulation conditions. The context-dependent function of PIM kinases is a key insight of the study.

results.result: IL-2 controls essential cytolytic effector and metabolic programs in CTL and is important for anti-viral immunity and cancer immunotherapy. PIM kinases mediate IL-2 control of glucose transporters, lipid metabolic enzymes, and key cytolytic proteins (granzymes A and B) in effector CD8 T cells.
results.evaluation: C90 is supported by literature citation and represents established knowledge. C91 is an inference from the proteomics data showing reduced expression of these proteins in Pim dKO CTL. The claim is well-supported, though the term 'mediate' implies a direct mechanistic role that may be more complex than simple transcriptional control, as shown by the mRNA/protein discordance data.

results.result: PIM kinases control protein expression primarily through regulation of protein translation rather than transcription. Loss of PIM kinase activity reduces protein synthesis rates in CTL (shown by OPP incorporation), though the reduction is modest. This mechanism has been reported previously in other cell types and explains the discordance between mRNA and protein changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C95 are supported by the combined RNAseq/proteomics analysis showing mRNA/protein discordance (C92) and OPP incorporation assays demonstrating reduced protein synthesis (C93, Figure 5M). The modest magnitude (C94) is acknowledged and contextualized with literature showing that modest changes can be functionally significant. Prior reports in other systems (C95) provide additional support.

results.result: Reduced protein synthesis in PIM kinase-deficient cells could result from reduced mTORc1 activity combined with increased expression of the translational repressor PDCD4. Additionally, protein synthesis is energetically demanding, and reduced glucose transporter expression would limit glucose availability to fuel protein production.
results.evaluation: C96 is a reasonable inference from the data showing reduced mTORc1 activity (C74-C75) and increased PDCD4 (C124). C97 is established biological knowledge. Together, these provide a plausible mechanistic model, though the relative contributions of each factor are not quantified. The model is consistent with all available data.

results.result: PIM kinases are required for IL-2 to fully repress expression of lymph node homing receptors (CD62L, CCR7, S1PR1) in effector CD8 T cells. These molecules control T cell homing to secondary lymphoid tissue, and IL-2 normally induces their downregulation to redirect effector cells away from lymphoid tissues. IL-2 maintained Pim dKO effector T cells retain the capacity to home to secondary lymphoid tissues in vivo.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C102 synthesize the molecular findings (increased homing receptor expression) with functional validation (adoptive transfer) and established knowledge of receptor function (C99-C100). The conclusion that PIM kinases mediate IL-2 repression of the naive trafficking program (C101) is well-supported by the data.

results.result: Loss of PIM kinases does not cause IL-2 differentiated effector T cells to fully switch to a memory phenotype. Pim dKO CTL do not re-express key memory markers (TCF7, IL-7 receptor), lack a memory mitochondrial proteome, and cluster more closely with IL-2 WT CTL than IL-15 CTL by PCA. Thus, Pim1/Pim2-deficiency prevents optimal effector differentiation without causing full memory conversion.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C106 are supported by proteomics and RNAseq data (Supplementary files 2 and 6, Figure 5—figure supplement 1). The PCA analysis (C105) provides quantitative support for the conclusion. This is an important clarification that the lymph node homing phenotype does not reflect complete memory differentiation, addressing a potential alternative interpretation.

results.result: Pan-PIM kinase inhibitors are in development as anti-cancer drugs, and it has been suggested that PIM inhibitors might be used to generate more stem-memory-like CD8 T cells for cancer immunotherapy.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C108 are supported by literature citations (Chatterjee et al., 2019; Clements and Warfel, 2022) and represent the translational context for the study. These claims establish the clinical relevance of understanding PIM kinase function in T cells.

results.result: PIM kinases show selective function for IL-2 versus IL-15 in conventional CD8 T cells, contrasting with their role in intestinal IEL where they direct IL-15 control of metabolic programming. In IEL, IL-15 alone strongly induces PIM expression, whereas in conventional CD8 T cells, IL-15 does not sustain high PIM levels. High PIM expression alone is not predictive of functional importance, as shown by high PIM levels in TCR-activated cells without functional impact.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C113 synthesize the current findings with prior work (James et al., 2021) to explain apparent discrepancies. The differential PIM expression in IL-15 conditions (C112) is supported by proteomics data (Figure 3A). The insight about expression levels not predicting function (C113) is an important conceptual point supported by the TCR activation data.

results.result: PIM kinases are required to maximally stimulate mTORc1 activity in IL-2 expanded CTL, contradicting prior suggestions that mTORc1 compensates for PIM kinase deficiency. This examination reveals cell context-dependent regulatory roles for PIM kinases rather than universal functions across all T cell stimulation conditions.
results.evaluation: C114 is supported by western blot and flow cytometry data (Figure 6A-B) showing reduced mTORc1 activity in Pim dKO cells. C115 is a well-justified synthesis of the findings showing differential PIM kinase requirements across TCR, IL-15, and IL-2 conditions. This represents an important conceptual advance in understanding PIM kinase biology.

results.result: RNAseq of IL-2 expanded CTL quantified ~14,000 RNA with 223 decreased and 155 increased by Pim1/Pim2 deficiency (FC >1.5, q<0.05). Some protein changes (perforin, Granzymes C-G, K) corresponded to mRNA changes, but striking examples showed protein decreases without mRNA changes (Granzymes A and B, glucose transporters SLC2A1 and SLC2A3). ~75% of proteins with changed expression showed no strong mRNA changes (FC <1.2), and only 17 of ~500 decreased proteins showed corresponding mRNA decreases.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C122 are supported by parallel RNAseq and proteomics analysis (Figure 5A-G, Supplementary files 6-7). The quantitative analysis of mRNA/protein concordance is rigorous and clearly demonstrates post-transcriptional regulation. This is a key mechanistic finding that explains how PIM kinases control effector function.

results.result: Multiple lines of evidence support PIM kinase control of protein translation: small reduction in ribosome content scaling with total protein reduction, increased translational repressor PDCD4 (confirmed by flow cytometry and underpinned by mRNA), increased PDCD4 after 24hr PIM inhibitor treatment, decreased EIF4A1, and approximate halving of the EIF4A1:PDCD4 ratio. PDCD4 inhibits translation by binding EIF4A1 in a 2:1 ratio. 24hr treatment with PIM inhibitors caused quantitative reduction in protein synthesis rates (OPP incorporation).
results.evaluation: Claims C123-C130 provide converging evidence for the translational control mechanism through multiple approaches: proteomics (Figure 5H-L), flow cytometry validation (Figure 5J), pharmacological inhibition (Figure 4—figure supplement 2F), and direct protein synthesis measurement (Figure 5M). The mechanistic model involving PDCD4 and EIF4A1 is supported by established knowledge (C127) and quantitative data (C128). This is a comprehensive mechanistic analysis.

results.result: CD8 T cells express ~200 Serine/Threonine kinases. PIM kinases are constitutively active, with their signaling participation dictated by regulated protein expression. PIM1 and PIM2 have little expression in naive T cells but are induced by TCR activation, costimulation, and are direct transcriptional targets of JAK/STAT pathways downstream of diverse cytokines.
results.evaluation: Claims C131-C134 are supported by literature citations and represent established knowledge that provides important context for the study. These claims are consistent with the experimental data showing regulated PIM expression in response to different stimuli.

results.result: Prior work has reported various roles for PIM kinases in T cells: mild reduction in proliferation with sub-optimal TCR/IL-2 stimulation, control of survival pathways in naive T cells with mTORc1, promotion of stemness/memory transcription factors (Bcl6, Tcf7) upon deletion, maintenance of memory T cell survival, and prevention of mTORc1 activation and IEL proliferation in response to IL-15.
results.evaluation: Claims C135-C139 accurately cite prior literature and provide important context for interpreting the current findings. These claims establish the existing knowledge base and highlight areas of agreement and disagreement with the current study.

results.result: PIM kinases have clinical relevance: elevated expression in autoimmune conditions (rheumatoid arthritis, uveitis, coeliac disease) with proposed therapeutic inhibition; PIM inhibitors in cancer clinical trials (not effective as monotherapy); studies showing PIM inhibition reduces PD-L1 on tumor cells/macrophages; but PIM inhibition is generally inhibitory for T cell activation, proliferation, and effector activities, potentially diminishing anti-tumor responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C140-C145 are supported by literature citations and represent the translational context and clinical implications of the work. These claims establish why understanding PIM kinase function in T cells is important for therapeutic development, highlighting both potential benefits and risks of PIM inhibition.

results.result: PIM1 and PIM2 kinases are rapidly induced at both protein and mRNA levels following TCR engagement in CD8 T cells, with PIM1 appearing within 3 hours and PIM2 by 9 hours, sustained at 24 hours. PIM3 is minimally expressed, confirming PIM1 and PIM2 as the major PIM kinases in activated T cells.
results.evaluation: All reviewers explicitly acknowledge these findings. Reviewer 1 states 'PIM1 protein was induced within 3 hours of TCR engagement and its expression was sustained at least up to 24 hours. The kinetics of PIM2 expression was protracted as compared to that of PIM1.' Reviewer 2 confirms 'PIM1/2 are upregulated in response to T-cell activation.' No concerns were raised about these expression kinetics data.

results.result: Pim dKO mice showed normal proportions of peripheral T cells in spleens, but reduced total numbers of T cells and splenocytes, likely due to smaller body size of the knockout mice.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 notes 'Pim1/Pim2 double knockout (Pim dKO) mice were generated on a B6 background and found to express lower number of splenocytes' without raising concerns. The interpretation about body size is accepted as consistent with previous literature on PIM-deficient mice.

results.result: PIM kinases are dispensable for TCR/CD28-driven T cell activation, as Pim dKO T cells showed normal cell size increase, activation marker upregulation (CD25, CD44, CD71), IFNγ production, and proliferation over 3 days. Proteomics analysis of >7000 proteins revealed no substantial differences between WT and Pim dKO activated T cells, and rapamycin experiments showed no evidence of mTORc1 compensation.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly states 'No difference in TCR/CD28-driven proliferation was observed between WT and Pim dKO T cells over 3 days in culture. Quantitative proteomics of >7000 proteins further revealed no substantial quantitative or qualitative differences in protein content or proteome composition. Therefore, other signaling pathways can compensate for the lack of PIM kinases downstream of TCR activation.' Reviewer 2 confirms 'PIM1/2 did not significantly influence T-cell activation, proliferation, or expression of anything in the proteome under anti-CD3/CD28 driven activation.'

results.result: IL-15 upregulates PIM1 and PIM2 expression in antigen-primed CD8 T cells, but PIM kinases are largely dispensable for IL-15-driven memory T cell differentiation. Pim dKO cells showed only a moderate (~4-fold) proliferative disadvantage in IL-15, with no impact on viability. RNAseq and proteomics analyses revealed minimal transcriptional and proteomic changes, including normal expression of memory markers (CD62L, CCR7, S1PR1, TCF7, FOXO1, KLF2, ID3) and indistinguishable mitochondrial proteome composition.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 states 'Analysis of the survival, proliferation, proteome, and transcriptome of Pim dKO CD8 T cells kept for 6 days in IL-15 showed that PIM1 and PIM2 are dispensable to drive the IL-15-mediated metabolic or differentiation programs of antigen-primed CD8 T cells.' Reviewer 2 notes 'This is perhaps somewhat surprising given PIM1/2 are upregulated, albeit to a small degree, in response to IL-15, and yet PIM1/2 did not seem to influence CD8+ T cell differentiation towards a memory state.' Both reviewers accept these findings without challenge.

results.result: IL-2 induces higher PIM1 expression than IL-15 in CD8 T cells. Pim dKO cells responded normally to IL-2 for STAT5 phosphorylation, CD25 expression, and viability, with only a mild (~2-fold) proliferative disadvantage and normal expression of activation markers CD44 and CD71.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 notes 'Pim1/Pim2-deficiency had no impact on the ability of IL-2 to maintain CD8 T cell viability and proliferation' while acknowledging the mild proliferative difference. These findings are accepted without criticism by all reviewers.

results.result: PIM kinases are required for IL-2 to fully repress expression of lymphoid homing receptors CD62L, CCR7, and S1PR1 in effector CTL. Pim dKO CTL sustained higher CD62L expression and increased mRNA levels of Sell, Klf2, Ccr7, and S1pr1. Consequently, Pim dKO CTL retained capacity to home to secondary lymphoid organs (lymph nodes and spleen) after adoptive transfer, unlike WT CTL.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly states 'WT CTL downregulated expression of CD62L whereas the Pim dKO CTL sustained higher CD62L expression' and 'the differences between Pim dKO and WT CTL in terms of CD62L expression resulted in that Pim dKO CTL but not WT CTL retained the capacity to home to secondary lymphoid organs.' Reviewer 2 confirms 'Loss of PIM1/2 made T cells...with a surface profile that maintained homing towards secondary lymphoid tissue' and notes the in vivo adoptive transfer experiments showed 'PIM1/2KO cells homed better to secondary lymphoid tissue.'

results.result: Proteomics analysis of IL-2 expanded CTL revealed that Pim dKO cells had reduced total protein mass and 513 downregulated proteins, including glucose transporters (SLC2A1, SLC2A3), lipid biosynthesis enzymes (SCD2, HMGCS1, MVK, IDI1, FDPS, FDFT1, SQLE), and key effector proteins (granzymes, perforin, IFNγ, TNFα). Pim dKO CTL were smaller and less granular but maintained an effector-like transcription factor profile (high TBX21, low TCF1) and mitochondrial proteome. PIM kinase inhibitors (PIM447, AZD1208) recapitulated these effects.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 states 'Comparison of the proteome of day 6 IL-2 cultured WT and Pim dKO CTL showed that the latter expressed lower levels of the glucose transporters, SLC2A1 and SLC2A3, of a number of proteins involved in fatty acid and cholesterol biosynthesis, and CTL effector proteins such as granzymes, perforin, IFNg and TNFa.' Reviewer 2 confirms 'Using proteomics, they saw...reduced expression of metabolism-related proteins (e.g., GLUT1/3 & cholesterol biosynthesis) and effector-function related proteins (e.g., IFNy and granzymes).' Both reviewers accept these findings as robust.

results.result: RNAseq analysis of IL-2 expanded CTL showed 223 decreased and 155 increased mRNA in Pim dKO cells. Critically, ~75% of proteins with changed expression showed no corresponding mRNA changes, with only 17 of ~500 downregulated proteins showing concordant mRNA decreases. This discordance revealed that PIM kinases primarily control protein expression post-transcriptionally rather than transcriptionally.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly notes 'Parallel transcriptomics analysis showed that the reduced expression of perforin and some granzymes correlated with a decrease in their mRNA whereas the decreased protein levels of granzymes B and A, and of the glucose transporters SLC2A1 and SLC2A3 did not correspond with decreased mRNA expression.' Reviewer 2 states 'Rather neatly, by performing both RNA-seq and proteomics on the same IL-2 stimulated WT vs. PIM1/2 KO cells, the authors found that changes at the proteome level were not corroborated by differences in RNA uncovering that PIM1/2 predominantly influence protein synthesis/translation.' The editor highlights 'It's also noteworthy that Pim1/Pim2 impact is better revealed through quantitative proteomics than transcriptomics.'

results.result: PIM kinases control protein synthesis rates in IL-2 expanded CTL. Pim dKO CTL showed reduced ribosome content, increased translational repressor PDCD4, decreased EIF4A1, and an approximate halving of the EIF4A1:PDCD4 ratio. Treatment with PIM kinase inhibitors (PIM447, AZD1208) caused quantitative reduction in protein synthesis rates measured by OPP incorporation, confirming PIM kinase effects operate via translational control.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 states 'Therefore, PIM kinases are likely required for IL-2 to maximally control protein synthesis in CD8 CTL. Along that line, the translational repressor PDCD4 was increased in Pim dKO CTL and pan-PIM kinase inhibitors caused a reduction in protein synthesis rates in IL-2 expanded CTL.' Reviewer 2 notes 'I particularly liked their use of matched RNA-seq and proteomics to first suggest that PIM1/2 kinases may predominantly influence translation (then going on to verify this via their protein translation experiment - although I must add this was only done using PIM kinase inhibitors not the PIM1/2KO cells).' The verification using inhibitors is accepted as supporting evidence.

results.result: The proteome remodeling in Pim dKO CTL shared features with mTORc1 inhibition (increased PDCD4, decreased cholesterol biosynthesis and effector molecules). Pim1/Pim2-deficiency modestly reduced mTORc1 activity in IL-2 maintained CD8 T cells, as shown by reduced pS6K T389 and IL-2-induced S6 phosphorylation, though S6 phosphorylation in response to phorbol esters/calcium ionophores remained intact. PIM kinases were required to maximally stimulate mTORc1 activity rather than mTORc1 compensating for PIM loss.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 accepts these findings without criticism. The connection to mTORc1 is presented as mechanistic insight explaining the proteome changes. The data showing reduced mTORc1 activity markers in Pim dKO cells is accepted as supporting the model that PIM kinases act upstream or in parallel to mTORc1.

results.result: Despite retaining lymphoid homing capacity, Pim dKO CTL do not fully switch to a memory phenotype. They do not re-express key memory markers like TCF7 and IL-7 receptor, lack a memory mitochondrial proteome, and PCA analysis shows Pim dKO IL-2 expanded CTL cluster more closely with WT IL-2 CTL than with IL-15 expanded memory cells. Thus, Pim1/Pim2-deficiency prevents optimal effector differentiation without causing full memory conversion.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly states 'this thorough and solid study showed that the PIM1/2 kinases shape the effector CD8 T cell proteomes rather than transcriptomes' and accepts the conclusion that loss of PIM kinases impairs effector differentiation without causing memory conversion. Reviewer 2 notes 'Effectively, PIM1/2 knockout reduced the differentiation of CD8+ T cells towards an effector state' and accepts the nuanced interpretation that these are not fully memory cells.

results.result: The study reveals context-dependent roles for PIM kinases: they have no effect on TCR/CD28-driven programs, very little impact on IL-15-driven memory differentiation, but are required for IL-2 programming of effector CTL differentiation, specifically mediating IL-2 control of glucose transporters, lipid metabolic enzymes, and cytolytic proteins. This demonstrates cell context-dependent regulatory roles rather than universal functions.
results.evaluation: The editor states these are 'important findings' that 'detail the role of Pim1 and Pim2 in controlling the behaviour and activity of 'killer' T cells.' Reviewer 1 concludes 'this thorough and solid study showed that the PIM1/2 kinases shape the effector CD8 T cell proteomes rather than transcriptomes and are important mediators of IL2-signalling and CD8 T cell trafficking.' Reviewer 2 notes 'they hint towards a more general finding that kinases may have distinct behaviour in different T-cell subtypes/states' and calls it 'a nice addition to our understanding of how serine/threonine kinases impact T cell state.'

results.result: The selectivity of PIM kinases for IL-2 versus IL-15 responses in conventional CD8 T cells contrasts with their role in intestinal IEL, where they mediate IL-15-driven metabolic programming. This discrepancy may be explained by differential PIM kinase expression levels: IL-15 does not sustain high PIM levels in conventional CD8 T cells, whereas in IEL, IL-15 alone strongly induces PIM expression. High PIM expression alone is not predictive of functional importance.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly notes 'Even more surprising is that IL-15 was previously shown to influence the metabolic programming of intestinal intraepithelial lymphocytes, suggesting cell-type specific effects from PIM kinases.' The authors' explanation based on differential PIM expression levels is accepted as a reasonable interpretation of the discrepancy between cell types.

results.result: The findings have translational implications: PIM kinase inhibitors are in clinical development for cancer and have been proposed for autoimmunity and to generate memory-like T cells for immunotherapy. However, the current data show that PIM inhibition does not cause full memory conversion and may diminish effector T cell responses, which is important context for therapeutic applications.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 notes 'I also liked that they used small molecule inhibitors to acutely reduce PIM1/2 activity, which corroborated some of their mouse knockout findings - this experiment helps resolve any findings resulting from potential adaptation issues from the PIM1/2 global knockout in mice but also gives it a more translational link given the potential use of PIM kinase inhibitors in the clinic.' The translational relevance is accepted as an important aspect of the work.

comparisons.comparison: Both evaluate PIM1/2 expression kinetics during T cell activation (C1-C8). OpenEval emphasizes temporal dynamics and data quality. Peer review confirms these findings explicitly, with Reviewer 1 noting PIM1 induction within 3 hours and sustained expression. Peer review also includes Pim3 absence claims (C9-C11) which OpenEval addresses separately in R2.

OpenEval R2 addresses Pim3 absence (C9-C11) with supporting RNAseq/proteomics data. Peer review R1 includes these claims in their broader evaluation of PIM expression patterns but does not specifically comment on Pim3, focusing instead on PIM1/2.

Perfect alignment on Pim dKO mouse characterization (C13-C16). Both accept the reduced splenocyte numbers and body size interpretation. OpenEval notes the inference about body size is reasonable despite lack of direct measurements; peer review accepts this without concern.

Strong agreement on TCR/CD28 activation findings (C17-C23). Both conclude PIM kinases are dispensable for TCR-driven responses. OpenEval emphasizes multiple orthogonal approaches; peer review explicitly quotes the compensation by other signaling pathways. Peer review R3 also includes some IL-2 proliferation claims (C26-C30) not in OpenEval R4.
